issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' is hard to reconcile with simultaneously becoming so overwhelmed on recall that she has to stop and experiencing intense rage when remembering. Mild coexistence is possible, but 'very easily' directly opposes marked emotional disorganization on recall and is clinically inconsistent within the same node.

issues.item: Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy 'Avoid Police' is poorly aligned with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a combat trauma in a 21-year-old nurse, avoidance of police is not supported by the listed triggers, threat items, or memory content, which center on sirens, bodily arousal, transport, flashbacks, scanning, and rage/overwhelm. This looks like a strategy targeting a threat context not otherwise represented in the formulation or symptom profile.

Avoiding police is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a combat trauma survivor who is a nurse. The other selected items center on alarm, flashbacks, sirens, somatic arousal, and generalized danger scanning, but nothing else suggests police-specific threat, authority-related trauma meaning, or a law-enforcement context. This strategy appears disconnected from the trigger, threat, and memory content.

Bus riding as a selected trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear clinical link to the other chosen items. The active formulation strongly links triggers with threat and maladaptive strategies, yet the other trigger items are sirens and heart racing, and the threat/memory items emphasize flashbacking, rage, overwhelm, and danger scanning without any transport-related cueing. As selected here, this item feels insufficiently anchored to the rest of the combat-related profile.

vignette:
Aroha Tane is a 21-year-old New Zealand Māori woman who grew up in a close-knit family in Auckland before emigrating to the United States at eighteen to pursue nursing. Driven by a sense of duty that her whānau had always described as her defining quality, she enrolled in an accelerated nursing programme and, in her second year, accepted a placement with a military medical unit supporting forward operating personnel overseas. She had wanted, she later told her intake clinician, to do something that mattered. What she encountered during a seven-month deployment changed the architecture of her inner life in ways she is still struggling to name.

The incident that organises her current presentation occurred during a mass casualty event at a field medical station. A coordinated attack brought in wave after wave of critically injured soldiers over the course of several hours. Aroha was working triage when an explosion detonated close enough to shake the structure. The concussive blast was followed immediately by the shriek of emergency alert sirens, and in the chaos that followed she worked over a soldier whose chest wound was beyond saving. She performed compressions until her arms gave out, feeling his heart stop beneath her palms, and she remembers with terrible precision the moment her own pulse became indistinguishable from the effort - hammering so hard in her chest that she could not tell where her body ended and his began. The sirens did not stop for nearly forty minutes.

She returned to the United States eight months ago and took a position in the emergency department of a mid-sized urban hospital, believing that staying busy and staying useful would hold things together. For a while, the logic seemed to hold. Then the symptoms found their footing.

In the ED, ambulances arrive with sirens still cycling down, and the sound moves through Aroha before she can prepare for it. On two occasions she has found herself crouched behind a supply cart, certain in her body if not entirely in her mind that the attack was resuming - that the noise meant incoming, that she needed to get low. Her colleagues have noticed. Her charge nurse has asked, carefully, whether she is sleeping. She has said yes. The more disruptive pattern, though, is the one that surfaces when she is simply standing at a patient's bedside and her own heart rate climbs during a difficult procedure. The racing of her pulse has become a cue she cannot override. What frightened her most, she explained haltingly in her first session, was that she couldn't always tell whether the fear was a memory or a fact.

Outside work, Aroha has quietly dismantled the parts of her life that once carried joy. She stopped going to the gym months ago, because the elevated heart rate she felt on the treadmill was one she had come to associate with something she did not want to revisit. She has declined birthday gatherings and a trip her partner, Daniel, planned to celebrate their anniversary. She had come to believe, in a way she could not fully articulate, that allowing herself to feel good was a kind of exposure she could not afford - as though happiness had become its own threat, a state too open, too unguarded. Daniel has grown quieter around her. She has noticed him choosing his words carefully, and she understands, without being able to say it aloud, that the distance between them is widening.

When the memory of that night surfaces - and it surfaces often, without warning, with a vividness that collapses time - Aroha does not feel grief. She feels rage so complete it frightens her, and then an overwhelm so total that she has to put down whatever she is holding and leave the room. She knows what happened. She was there for every second of it. But when her clinician asked her to describe it, she sat for a long time looking at her hands. She knows what happened, she said finally. She just cannot find the words.

What brought her in was a near-miss: she snapped at a junior nurse in front of a patient's family, loudly and without proportion, and walked off the floor. She sat in the stairwell for twenty minutes, scanning the door. She is afraid, she says, that she is becoming someone she does not recognise. She hopes, more than anything, that she is not.
